Part 1 of 7

Why the Great War Began

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 1: Assess the causes of the Great War and how the United States responded initially to the outbreak of hostilities.

IN MY WORDS: In your own words, what were two causes of the Great War?

Reading ATwo Armed Camps

In the race for arms and influence, the competitors divided into separate military alliances: the Triple Alliance (called the Central Powers during the war), consisting of Germany, Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria, and Turkey (the Ottoman Empire); and the Triple Entente (later called the Allied Powers), composed of France, Great Britain, Russia, and, later, Italy. The members of these two alliances pledged to defend each other, thus dividing Europe into two armed camps.

These four factors—industrialization, nationalism, imperialism, and militarism—created a combustible situation. All that was needed to ignite it was a spark.

Word help: alliances = groups of nations that promise to help each other · pledged = promised · combustible = ready to explode · ignite = set on fire · imperialism = building empires by taking other lands

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “An Uneasy Neutrality” (The Great War) (p. 907).

Reading BThe Spark and the Western Front

When Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, announced he would visit Sarajevo (the capital of Austrian-controlled Bosnia), militant Serbian nationalists plotted to assassinate him. On June 28, 1914, Ferdinand and his pregnant wife, Sophie, paraded through the streets of Sarajevo in an open car. When the archduke’s driver took a wrong turn and was forced to back the car down a crowded street, Gavrilo Princip, a nineteen-year-old Serbian nationalist, shot and killed the imperial couple.

German troops then invaded neutral Belgium to gain easier access to France, murdering or deporting thousands of civilians in the process. The “rape of Belgium” brought its ally, Great Britain, into the war on August 4. The Allied armies were concentrated on the Western Front, the battle line in northern France and Belgium.

Word help: heir = the person next in line to be king or emperor · assassinate = murder a leader · deporting = forcing people out of a country · neutral = not taking sides

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “An Uneasy Neutrality” (The Great War).

MapMap 21.1: The Great War in Europe, 1914

This modern textbook map shows which countries joined each side when the war began in 1914.

Map key: Orange = Central Powers (Triple Alliance) · Green = Allied Powers (Triple Entente) · Tan = neutral countries (not fighting) · Sarajevo = city where the archduke was killed

Norton, Ch. 21, Map 21.1, “The Great War in Europe, 1914.” Modern textbook map.

Map evidence. (1) Name two Central Powers on the map. (2) Germany sits between two Allied Powers. Name them. (3) Why would that make fighting hard for Germany?

Reading CTrench Warfare

In the early weeks of the war, German armies swept across Belgium and northeastern France, only to bog down in nightmarish trench warfare that came to symbolize the war’s futility and horror. Both sides dug in and fought a grinding war of attrition, gaining little territory in the process of unprecedented casualties.

In one assault against the Germans in Belgium, the British lost 13,000 men in three hours—and gained only 100 yards.

Machine guns, submarines, aerial bombing, poison gas, flame throwers, land mines, mortars, long-range artillery, and armored tanks changed the nature of warfare.

Word help: futility = uselessness · war of attrition = wearing the enemy down until it runs out of men and supplies · casualties = soldiers killed or wounded · unprecedented = never seen before

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “An Uneasy Neutrality” (Trench Warfare; An Industrial War) (p. 908).

Part 2 of 7

From Neutral to War

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 1: Assess the causes of the Great War and how the United States responded initially to the outbreak of hostilities.

IN MY WORDS: At first, did the United States join the war? What finally pulled it in?

Reading DNeutral in Name Only

President Wilson urged Americans to remain “neutral in thought as well as in action.” Privately, however, he worked to ensure that the United States could provide Great Britain and France as much financial assistance and as many supplies as possible.

By the spring of 1915, the Allied Powers’ desperate need for food, supplies, and weapons had generated an economic windfall for U.S. companies, bankers, and farmers. . . . Banks and other investors would eventually send more than $2 billion to the Allied Powers while offering only $27 million to Germany.

The disproportionate financial assistance provided to the Allies revealed that the United States was neutral in name only.

Word help: neutral = not taking sides · windfall = sudden large profit · investors = people who put in money to make more money · disproportionate = much bigger for one side

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “An Uneasy Neutrality” (Initial American Reactions; Supporting the Allies) (p. 910).

Picture 1“The Sandwich-Board Man”

This political cartoon shows Uncle Sam (the United States) wearing a sign on his front and a sign on his back. (It is a primary source.)

What to look for: Uncle Sam = a symbol of the United States · sandwich board = two signs worn on the front and back · ammunition = bullets and shells · orders filled promptly = we ship fast

Norton, Ch. 21, “An Uneasy Neutrality,” caption: “To illustrate America’s peculiar brand of neutrality, this political cartoon shows Uncle Sam wearing a sandwich board that advertises the nation’s conflicting desires to remain out of the war while profiting from it.” Primary source.

Picture 1. What does the front sign say? What does the back sign say? What is the cartoonist saying about American neutrality?

Reading EU-Boats and the Lusitania

The Germans made unprecedented use of a terrifying new implement of war: U-boats (Unterseeboote in German), or submarines. The Germans were the first to employ them in large numbers. During 1915, German U-boats sank 227 British ships in the Atlantic Ocean and North Sea.

On May 7, 1915, a German submarine off the Irish coast fired a single torpedo that sank the British passenger ship Lusitania, the largest, fastest, and most luxurious ocean liner in the world. Of the 1,198 persons on board who died, 128 were Americans. Fifty of the dead were infants.

On January 31, 1917, German military leaders ordered that unrestricted submarine warfare in the Atlantic resume the next day. Now, all American vessels headed for Britain, France, or Italy could be sunk without warning.

Word help: unprecedented = never done before · implement = tool · torpedo = an underwater bomb fired by a submarine · ocean liner = a big passenger ship · resume = start again

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “An Uneasy Neutrality” (Neutral Rights and Submarine Attacks; America Goes to War).

Reading FThe Zimmermann Telegram and War

On February 3, 1917, President Wilson informed Congress that, in order to preserve the “dignity and honor of the United States,” he had formally ended diplomatic relations with the German government. Three weeks later, on February 25, he learned that the British had intercepted a coded telegram from Germany’s foreign minister, Arthur Zimmermann, to the German ambassador in Mexico City. The telegram said that if war erupted with the United States, the ambassador was to offer the Mexican government an alliance: If Mexican forces would invade the United States, in exchange, at the conclusion of the war, Germany would return to Mexico its “lost territory in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona.”

On March 1, newspapers broke the news of the Zimmermann telegram. The Mexican government immediately disavowed any support for the Germans, but the German attempt to recruit Mexico as an ally so infuriated Americans that many called for war.

On April 2, 1917, the president asked Congress to declare war against the German Empire and its allies. “The world must be made safe for democracy,” he said, in one of the most memorable speeches of his presidency.

Word help: intercepted = caught before it arrived · ambassador = a country’s official in another country · alliance = a partnership · infuriated = made very angry · democracy = government by the people

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “An Uneasy Neutrality” (The Zimmermann Telegram; Wilson Declares War).

Part 3 of 7

The Home Front

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 2: Explain how the Wilson administration’s efforts to mobilize the nation for war affected American society.

IN MY WORDS: Name one group whose life changed during the war, and tell how.

Reading GSoldiers, Factories, and Women Workers

In April 1917, the U.S. Army remained small, untested, and poorly armed. With just 127,000 men, it was only the seventeenth-largest army in the world. . . . On May 18, Congress passed the Selective Service Act, which instructed men ages twenty-one to thirty to register for the draft (later expanded to ages eighteen to forty-five years).

Removing millions of men from the workforce for service in the armed forces created an acute labor shortage across the United States during 1917. To meet it, the government and businesses encouraged women to take jobs previously held by men. One government poster shouted: “For Every Fighter, a Woman Worker.” . . . women were recruited to work on farms, loading docks, and railway crews; as well as in the armaments industry, machine shops, steel and lumber mills, and chemical plants.

Word help: draft = a law that makes men join the military · recruited = asked to join · armaments = weapons · acute labor shortage = not nearly enough workers

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “Mobilizing for War” (Managing the Home Front; A New Labor Force) (p. 916).

Reading HBlack Soldiers and the Great Migration

Eventually, more than 400,000 Blacks joined the army or navy (they were not allowed in the Marines), where they were required to serve in racially segregated units commanded by White officers.

The most significant development in African American life during the early twentieth century was the Great Migration northward from the South. . . . The first great wave of Black migrants left the South in 1915–1916, when rapidly expanding war industries needed new workers.

In the North, for the most part, African Americans were able to speak more freely and were treated better than they had been in the South, and educational opportunities for children were much better. Importantly, in the North, Blacks were able to vote. . . . they were often forced into substandard and segregated housing and received lower wages than Whites.

Word help: segregated = separated by race · migrants = people who move to a new place · substandard = poor, below normal quality

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “Mobilizing for War” (Race, Ethnicity, and the War; The Great Migration).

Reading IA Loss of Civil Liberties

Once the United States entered the war, Americans equated anything German with disloyalty.

Woodrow Wilson, who had long presented himself as a protector of civil liberties, pressed Congress to pass the Espionage and Sedition Acts, which gave the president extraordinary authority to punish critics of the war effort. . . . A year later, Congress amended the Espionage Act with the Sedition Act. It outlawed saying, writing, or printing anything “disloyal, profane, scurrilous, or abusive” about the American form of government, the Constitution, or the army and navy.

The criminalizing of opposition to the war by the Espionage and Sedition Acts made it clear that the Wilson administration regarded many American citizens as enemies of the United States.

Word help: civil liberties = basic freedoms, like free speech · disloyalty = not being faithful to your country · critics = people who speak against something · profane, scurrilous = rude and insulting · criminalizing = making it a crime

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “Mobilizing for War” (A Loss of Civil Liberties; Waging War on Labor Radicals).

Part 4 of 7

Winning the War

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 3: Explain how the American war effort contributed to the defeat of the Central Powers.

Core Objective 4: Evaluate how Americans and Europeans reacted to Wilson’s plans for a peaceful world order as outlined in his Fourteen Points.

IN MY WORDS: How did American troops help end the war? What did Wilson want the peace to look like?

Reading JAmericans on the Western Front

The American role in repelling the German offensive was crucial. So was their role in the counterattack that began in August 1918. On September 26, American troops joined British and French armies in a drive toward Sedan, France, and its strategic railroad that supplied the German army. With 1.2 million U.S. soldiers involved, including some 180,000 African Americans, it was the largest American action of the war; and it resulted in 117,000 U.S. casualties, including 26,000 dead.

Along the entire French-Belgian front, however, the outnumbered Germans were in desperate retreat eastward across Belgium during the early fall of 1918. “America,” wrote German general Erich Ludendorff, “became the decisive power in the war.”

On November 9, the German kaiser resigned, and a republic was proclaimed. Then, on November 11 at 5:00 a.m., the nations at war reached an armistice (cease-fire agreement).

Word help: offensives = big attacks · repelling = pushing back · casualties = soldiers killed or wounded · decisive = deciding the outcome · kaiser = the German emperor · armistice = an agreement to stop fighting

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “The American Role in the War” (America Bolsters the Western Front; The End of the War).

Evidence. A German general wrote that America “became the decisive power in the war.” Give two facts from Reading J that support him.

Reading KWilson’s Fourteen Points

Woodrow Wilson was determined to ensure that the Great War would be the last world war. To that end, during 1917, he appointed a group of experts, called the Inquiry, to draft a peace plan. With their advice, Wilson developed what would come to be called the Fourteen Points, a comprehensive list of principles and provisions to guide international relations and shape the peace treaty.

The first five points called for the open conduct of diplomacy, the recognition of neutral nations’ right to continue maritime commerce in time of war (“freedom of the seas”), the removal of international trade barriers (free trade), the reduction of armaments, and the transformation of colonial empires into independent nations.

Point 14, the capstone of Wilson’s postwar scheme, envisioned “a general association of nations” (later called a “League of Nations”) to preserve global peace.

Word help: provisions = rules in an agreement · diplomacy = talks between countries · armaments = weapons · colonial empires = countries that rule other lands · capstone = the most important final part

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “The American Role in the War” (The End of the War).

Part 5 of 7

The Fight over the Peace

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 4: Evaluate how Americans and Europeans reacted to Wilson’s plans for a peaceful world order as outlined in his Fourteen Points.

IN MY WORDS: How did European leaders and the U.S. Senate react to Wilson’s peace plan?

Reading LThe Big Four and the Treaty of Versailles

The Big Four fought in private and in public. The British, led by Prime Minister David Lloyd George, and the French, under premier Georges Clemenceau (“the Tiger”), insisted that Wilson agree to their proposals to weaken Germany economically and militarily; while Vittorio Orlando, prime minister of Italy, focused on gaining territories from Austria.

The British and especially the French (on whose soil much of the war had been fought) wanted Germany to pay the entire financial cost of the war. On this point, Wilson made perhaps his most fateful concessions. He agreed to a clause in the peace treaty that forced Germany to accept responsibility for the war and its entire expense. The “war guilt” clause so offended Germans that it became a major factor in the rise of the Nazi Party during the 1920s.

Finally, on June 28, the Germans gave up and signed the treaty in the glittering Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. Thereafter, it was called the Treaty of Versailles.

Word help: prime ministers = leaders of governments · weaken = make weaker · fateful = with big results · concessions = things you give up in a deal · Nazi Party = the party Adolf Hitler later led

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “The Politics of Peace” (The Big Four; The Treaty of Versailles) (p. 930).

Source 1A British Delegate Judges Wilson (Primary Source)

John Maynard Keynes was a British delegate at the Paris Peace Conference. In 1920 he wrote a book about how Wilson did in the talks. Lloyd George was the British prime minister.

“The President was not a hero or a prophet; he was not even a philosopher; but a generously intentioned man, with many of the weaknesses of other human beings . . . What chance could such a man have against Mr. Lloyd George’s unerring, almost medium-like, sensibility to every one immediately round him? . . . But this blind and deaf Don Quixote was entering a cavern where the swift and glittering blade was in the hands of the adversary.”

Word help: prophet = a wise leader who sees the future · generously intentioned = meaning well · unerring = never wrong · medium-like = able to read minds · sensibility = awareness · Don Quixote = a story character who fights imaginary enemies · cavern = cave · adversary = enemy

John Maynard Keynes, The Economic Consequences of the Peace, 1920. In Norton, Ch. 21, “The Politics of Peace,” Comparing Perspectives: “The War and Its Aftermath” (p. 935).

Source 1. Keynes calls Wilson a “blind and deaf Don Quixote.” What is he saying about how Wilson did against the European leaders?

Point of view. Keynes was British, and he was at the peace talks. Why might he see Wilson differently than Wilson saw himself?

Reading MThe Senate Says No

Republican Henry Cabot Lodge, the powerful chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, opposed Wilson’s beloved League of Nations because it would potentially involve sending U.S. troops to foreign conflicts without congressional approval, a violation of the U.S. Constitution.

The final Senate vote in 1920 on Lodge’s revised treaty was 39 in favor and 55 against. The original treaty also lost, with 38 for and 53 against.

Treaty opponents, however, believed that they were simply returning America to its tradition of isolationism. The peoples of Europe had been fighting and killing each other for as long as anyone could remember, they argued. Why was that America’s business to solve?

Word help: congressional approval = permission from Congress · violation = breaking a rule · isolationism = staying out of other countries’ problems

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “The Politics of Peace” (The Treaty Ratification Debate; The Treaty under Attack).

Part 6 of 7

After the War

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 5: Analyze the war’s consequences for the United States, and its effects abroad.

IN MY WORDS: Name one good result and one bad result of the war for the United States.

Reading NA Deadly Flu and the Vote for Women

The disease appeared suddenly in the spring of 1918 at an army training base in Kansas, and it spread rapidly as ships carrying U.S. troops arrived in France. Its initial outbreak lasted a year and killed millions of people worldwide—twice as many as had died in the war. In the United States alone, it accounted for 670,000 deaths, over twelve times the number of U.S. combat deaths in France.

As the first outbreak of the Spanish flu was ending, women finally gained a constitutional guarantee of their right to vote. After six months of delay, debate, and failed votes, Congress passed the Nineteenth Amendment in the spring of 1919 and sent it to the states for ratification. It was no coincidence that it was during wartime, when women’s contributions to the war effort were so critical to American success, that a congressional majority finally took decisive action on the issue.

The Nineteenth Amendment became official on August 18, 1920. Women’s suffrage was the culmination of generations of activism and was the climactic achievement of the Progressive Era.

Word help: outbreak = a sudden spread of disease · constitutional guarantee = a right promised in the Constitution · ratification = approval by the states · culmination = the final high point · activism = working for a cause

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “Stumbling from War to Peace” (The Spanish Flu Pandemic; Women’s Suffrage at Last).

Reading OStrikes and Race Riots

In 1919, more than 4 million hourly-wage workers—20 percent of the workforce—participated in 3,600 strikes.

Yet the rising expectations among Black soldiers sparked a backlash among Whites, turning the postwar years into a tinderbox of racial tensions.

In 1919 alone, eighty-three African Americans, including nine military veterans, were lynched. What National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) leader James Weldon Johnson called the “Red Summer” (red signifying blood, not communism) began in July, when a mob of Whites invaded the Black neighborhood in Longview, Texas, angry over rumors of interracial dating. They burned shops and houses and ran several Black residents out of town.

Later that month, 38 people were killed and 537 injured in five days of rioting in Chicago. Some 50,000 African Americans, mostly migrants from the South, had moved to the city during the war. The Red Summer mocked the dreams of African Americans who had come north seeking a promised land.

Word help: strikes = workers refusing to work until they get better pay or hours · backlash = an angry reaction against something · tinderbox = something ready to catch fire · lynched = killed by a mob without a trial

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “Stumbling from War to Peace” (Economic Turbulence; Race Riots) (p. 939).

Reading PThe First Red Scare

Fears of revolution led to what came to be called the First Red Scare (another would occur in the 1950s).

On November 7, 1919, in what came to be called the “Palmer raids,” federal agents rounded up 450 alien “radicals,” most of whom were law-abiding Russian immigrants. All were deported to Russia without a court hearing. On January 2, 1920, federal agents and police in dozens of cities arrested 5,000 more suspects. The blatant disregard for the civil liberties of those arrested led novelist Katharine Fullerton Gerould to declare in Harper’s Magazine that America “is no longer a free country in the old sense.”

But the fears that fueled the First Red Scare never entirely subsided. They continued in various forms in the 1920s, stoking new restrictions on immigration and other reactionary political movements.

Word help: Red = Communist · radicals = people who want big, sudden changes · deported = sent out of the country · blatant disregard = openly ignoring · reactionary = wanting to go back to the old ways

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “Stumbling from War to Peace” (The First Red Scare).

Reading QEffects of the Great War

Postwar America was a much different story. For the first time, the United States had decisively intervened in a major European war. Though President Wilson’s vision of a principled international order had been stymied by domestic political opposition, many of his ideas remain a touchstone of American foreign policy to this day. Passage of the women’s suffrage amendment opened new doors for millions of Americans, yet many continued to suffer from intolerance, racial bigotry, and government-sanctioned oppression.

Despite postwar inflation, the American economy had emerged from the Great War largely unscathed. . . . The United States was now the world’s dominant economic power.

Word help: decisively intervened = stepped in and made a big difference · touchstone = a standard to measure by · bigotry = hatred of people who are different · unscathed = not hurt

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 21, “Stumbling from War to Peace” (Effects of the Great War).
